paragraphs: In August 2013, a group of journalists in London tasted a hamburger that had cost around a quarter of a million pounds to produce. It was not made from a cow, at least not in the usual way. The meat had been grown in a laboratory from cells taken from a living animal. The verdict of the tasters was polite rather than enthusiastic: close to meat, but not very juicy.

More than a decade later, cultivated meat, as its producers prefer to call it, has moved from science fiction to the shelves of a handful of restaurants. In 2020, Singapore became the first country to approve its sale, and in 2023 two companies received permission to sell cultivated chicken in the United States.

The process begins with a small sample of cells taken from an animal, usually without harming it. These cells are placed in large steel tanks called bioreactors, where they are fed a nutrient-rich liquid and multiply. The result can then be shaped into products such as nuggets or burgers.

Supporters point to several potential benefits. Animal farming uses a large share of the world's agricultural land and produces significant greenhouse gas emissions. Growing meat from cells could, in theory, require far less land and water, and it would avoid the slaughter of billions of animals every year.

However, many obstacles remain. Producing cultivated meat on a large scale is still extremely expensive, and some scientists doubt that costs will ever fall enough to compete with conventional meat. Its environmental benefits also depend on how much energy the bioreactors consume and where that energy comes from. Meanwhile, some governments have taken the opposite direction: Italy, for instance, banned its production and sale in 2023, partly to protect traditional farmers.

Then there is the question of taste and trust. Surveys suggest that many consumers are curious but hesitant about eating something grown in a tank. Whether cultivated meat becomes an everyday food or remains an expensive curiosity may depend less on scientists than on what ends up on our plates.
